title: Straining to urinate (especially a male cat)
signs: Repeated trips to the litter tray with little or no urine, crying, licking the genitals, hiding.
action: Emergency: see a vet immediately. Being unable to pass urine is a recognised emergency in cats.
source: Veterinary emergency triage guidance (e.g. GSVS); not yet verified against a primary source

title: Not eating for more than 24 hours
signs: Refuses all food. Kittens and overweight cats are at higher risk.
action: Call your vet the same day. A day or two without food can lead to hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver), especially in overweight cats; kittens, seniors and cats with chronic illness are at higher risk sooner.

title: Open-mouth or laboured breathing
signs: Panting at rest, open mouth, belly heaving, blue or pale gums.
action: Emergency: keep the cat calm and go to a vet or emergency clinic now.
source: Widely stated emergency sign; no specific source read yet

title: Lily exposure
signs: Any contact with true lilies (Lilium) or daylilies (Hemerocallis): leaves, petals, pollen on fur, or vase water, even without symptoms yet. Treat any plant called a lily as a risk.
action: Emergency: go to a vet immediately. Lilies can cause acute kidney failure within a few days; early treatment improves the chance of survival.

title: Dog flea or tick product containing permethrin
signs: Tremors, twitching, drooling, seizures after contact with a treated dog or product.
action: Emergency: contact a vet or the Animal Poisons Helpline now. Never use dog spot-ons on cats.
source: Australian vet clinic guidance (some dog tick/flea products contain permethrin, which can kill cats); not yet verified against RSPCA/AVA

title: Paralysis tick signs (east coast)
signs: Often subtle in cats: hiding, reluctance to jump, a changed or absent meow. Then wobbly or weak back legs, gagging or noisy breathing, vomiting. Signs can appear or worsen for 24–48 hours after a tick is removed.
action: Emergency: see a vet at once, even if you cannot find a tick. Tick paralysis can progress to breathing failure.
source: RSPCA Queensland; MSD Veterinary Manual (tick paralysis); Australian vet clinic guidance

title: Swallowed a human medicine or toxin
signs: Paracetamol or ibuprofen (cats are especially sensitive to paracetamol), antifreeze, rat bait, or chewed unknown plants.
action: Emergency: call a vet or the Animal Poisons Helpline immediately. Do not induce vomiting unless a vet tells you to.
source: Australian Veterinary Association warning on human pain killers; SASH vet guidance (via search)

title: Sudden hind-leg weakness or pain
signs: Sudden loss of use of one or both back legs, crying out, signs of pain. Can be a blood clot (aortic thromboembolism), often a complication of heart disease.
action: Emergency: contact your vet immediately and be ready to go now.
source: Veterinary clinic guidance and a feline aortic thromboembolism case report (via search); not a primary reference
